How caps were identified, and why not by order type

Order type cannot be used to identify caps — in any year

Caps were progressively written under Custom Embroidery across the whole decade, not just recently. Cap units as a share of order-type-21 volume went 8.0% in 2016 → 30.5% in 2025 → 53.4% in 2026. So the familiar “cap orders fell from 582 to 154” is largely a coding artifact: actual cap units went 40,342 to 21,379.

Caps are instead identified from the garment (cap, trucker, hat, beanie, visor, snapback, flexfit, OSFA, mesh back, knit cap) — a definition that holds regardless of how the order was coded. Validated against order type 1 in the years where type 1 is still trustworthy:

The pricing is sound. It is not being charged.

Cost basis and measured throughput

Non-material cost of $1,494,241 over 16,650 matched production hours gives $89.74 per production hour. Production logging covers only part of paid time, so the loaded rate that a chargeable hour has to carry is $285.92 — an uplift of 3.186×.

Throughput below is measured from the production log, not estimated: caps 20.0 pcs/hr and flat embroidery 13.7 pcs/hr at 72+. “Price covers” is the garment margin plus the decoration charge; “gap/pc” is that minus cost.

Corrected cost basis supersedes the $89.74 above

The $89.74 production hour used elsewhere on this page was wrong

It loaded all admin, executive, art and sales cost onto machine time. Two consequences: a 150-piece order absorbed 7.3× the overhead of a 4-piece order for consuming the same sales effort, and embroidery was charged as if it were the whole company when it is 27% of orders and 52% of revenue. Split properly, the machine hour is cheap and the order is expensive.

Payroll comes from the journal, non-payroll from the GL — the GL Detail export is missing most payroll and must not be used for it. NWCA owns its building, so there is no rent; property tax ($33,542/yr) is the only facility cost and where it sits barely moves the rate. ⚠ 2024 office non-payroll spiked to $531,497 against roughly $275,000 either side, unexplained — it alone lifts that year to $250 per order.

The paperwork costs about three times the stitching

A 24-piece order uses roughly $75 of machine time and $261 of order cost. NWCA is an order-processing business that happens to embroider — which is why per-piece pricing is the wrong instrument for most of the cost, and a minimum order or order-level fee is the right one.

They are 43% of all orders, so removing them from the sales denominator concentrates rep cost onto the orders reps actually work. Small orders are reorders 21 years

A flat minimum would land on your best customers

Two-thirds to three-quarters of every 1-7 order is a reorder, in every era back to 2006 — never below 63% in any single year. The median case is a 3-piece follow-up worth $90, placed 27 days after a 62-piece order, from a customer who spent $2,278 in the prior 90 days. 32% come back inside 14 days.

So the 1-7 tier is three different situations

what it isorders/yrtreatment
reorder within 90 days of a 24+ order126keep the $50 fee — it is short by only $45
reorder after a smaller prior order145judgement call — relationship exists but is thin
standalone — no recent order behind it130the case a minimum is for

The existing $50 fee is the right number for a genuine reorder: a re-run costs the blank, the machine time, the rep and Bradley — about $230 against $185 billed — because art is zero on an existing design and the office cost was already carried by the parent order. What is missing is the standalone case, where $50 covers roughly a fifth of the real cost.

A fill-in predicts an account that bills half as much next year

Tested against a control anchored on an identical order (48+ pieces, over $1,000; groups verified comparable). After a small fill-in, the next order clears $1,000 26% of the time against 34% for the control — but the dip is one order deep and 83% place another 24+ order within two years, the same as the control. What does not recover is the money: 12-month revenue of $3,053 against $6,080. ⚠ Association, not cause — a customer needing 3 pieces after a 100-piece run may simply be winding down. Use it as a sales trigger, not a fee.

What Caspio charges today

The engine prices every surface the same way: price = round_up(blank_case_cost ÷ 0.53 + decoration). The denominator is a margin divisor, so 0.53 means a 47% margin on the garment portion — and because decoration is added after that divisor, the tier break is a flat dollar amount no matter how expensive the garment is.

tiergarment decorationcap decorationsmall-order fee
1-7$18.00$17.00$50.00
8-23$18.00$17.00—
24-47$14.00$13.00—
48-71$13.00$11.00—
72+$12.00$9.50—

Consequence worth knowing on big-ticket bids: the ladder spread from 1–7 to 72+ is the same $6.00 on a $85 Carhartt as on a $4 tee. On the tee that is a 32% price range; on the Carhartt it is about 3.5%. Rounding is HalfDollarCeil_Final for garments and HalfDollarCeil_Final for caps.

The $50.00 small-order fee is baked into the unit price rather than shown as a line item, and it reaches only about a fifth of the orders small enough to warrant it.

Where the breaks belong solved, not estimated

The tier ladder is a staircase approximation to a cost curve. To know whether the steps are in the right places you first have to know the curve — specifically how much of an order's cost is fixed setup that does not shrink when the order does.

The cost curve: hours(q) = S + v × q

Fitted three independent ways. They agree on S, which is the number every recommendation below depends on.

fitfixed setup Svariable vR²n
Flats — pooled tier points1.279 hr/order0.06612 hr/pc0.9885
Caps — pooled tier points1.224 hr/order0.04550 hr/pc0.9855
Order level, type 211.138 hr0.07022 hr/pc0.6221,472
Order level, type 1 (with imprints)1.184 hr0.06318 hr/pc0.773285

sts_Setup is filled in on only 51 of 5,521 production-log rows, so setup cannot be read off the log — it has to be regressed out. Kornit and patch rows are excluded (different processes).

Every order carries about 1.28 hours of setup before a single garment runs

That is $114.75 at the direct rate, or $365.59 fully loaded. It is the same whether the order is for 4 pieces or 400, and it is the entire reason small orders behave differently.

Which is why cost per piece collapses early, then flattens

The breaks are clustered where the curve is flat and absent where it is steep

By 8 pieces, cost per piece has already fallen to 17% of its one-piece value — 87.5% of every efficiency gain that will ever be available. Yet the ladder has no break anywhere in 1–23, where cost falls roughly sixfold, and three breaks across 24–72+, where it falls about 30%. The 1–7 tier alone spans a 5.4× cost range at a single price.

What the optimiser picks instead

Choosing K intervals over an ordered domain to minimise weighted error is the 1-D k-segmentation problem, which dynamic programming solves optimally — there is no judgement call in it. Run against the real order-size distribution, it lands in the same place at every cost target tested:

target $150/hr2 / 4 / 8 / 18
target $200/hr2 / 4 / 8 / 26

what we charge today8 / 24 / 48 / 72

Steer toward 48, not 72

The 72 break is worth $10 per hour over 48–71 — about 3.1%. Moving a 24-piece order to 48 is worth nine times more. And the single most valuable move available is getting an order out of 1–7: that step is worth $91 per hour.

Read the absolute numbers carefully: at the $89.74 direct rate every tier clears, so 1–7 is not losing cash — it is the worst use of a constrained hour. The distance between $89.74 and the $285.92 loaded rate is a utilization problem (only about a third of embroidery hours log as productive), and no price change closes it.

The small-order fee

Today's $50.00 recovers 44% of the $114.75 setup it exists to cover, and it stops at 7 pieces — so 8–23 pays nothing toward setup at all. The natural ceiling is where fixed and variable cost cross, S/v = 19.3 pieces for flats (26.9 for caps): below that an order is mostly setup. The nearest existing tier boundary is 23, so extending the fee there needs no new break.

Reorders

66% of customers reorder and 95% of all orders come from repeat customers, with a median gap of 56 days (quartiles 19 and 180). So this is a repeat business, and the fee lands mostly on people who already buy from us.

A reorder is not cheaper to set up

Comparing like for like — only customers whose genuine first order falls inside the production-log window — a first order sets up in 1.299 hr (n=215) and later orders in 1.382 hr (n=857). There is no saving. An early-reorder discount cannot be funded from a setup saving, because the saving does not exist.

The prize is consolidation, not earliness. Two orders from one customer landing close together each pay a fresh 1.28-hour setup:

The reorder target: catch the second order before the first runs

At order entry, if the customer has ordered within 60 days, offer to combine — and ask what they need through the next quarter rather than taking the reorder as presented. One setup instead of two is $115 every time it lands. Merging only the pairs already falling inside 30 days would cut 1–7 orders from about 2,760 to 484.

Five rules, priced individually

Each rule is costed in isolation against the same 1,938 orders, so the figures do not double-count each other. Rule 1 needs no price change at all.

1

Charge the price that is already in Caspio

Bill at list. No new price, no Caspio edit, no customer conversation about a rate increase — just stop discounting below the table. This is the single largest item on the page and the only one that needs no decision.

$442,001over 24 months
2

Bring cap decoration up to garment parity

Caps are decorated at $9.50 to $17.00 against $12.00 to $18.00 for garments, while measured cap throughput is only about 1.5× garment throughput. The discount is larger than the productivity difference justifies.

$49,060over 24 months
3

Extend the small-order fee to 8–23

The $50.00 fee stops at 7 pieces, so 8–23 carries the same $18.00 decoration charge as 1–7 with nothing behind it. It is the weakest tier in the book (494 orders in the window).

$37,050over 24 months
4

Make the small-order fee actually land on 1–7

It is currently absorbed into the unit price and reaches roughly a fifth of eligible orders (578 orders in the window). Charging it as a visible line item is the fix.

$28,900over 24 months
5

Surcharge the cheap blanks

The blank price decides whether an order earns anything, because the garment margin is a percentage of a small number. Add $4.00 per piece under $4, $2.50 from $4–8, $1.00 from $8–15, nothing above — the expensive garments already carry themselves.

What this analysis cannot tell you

  • Production logging stopped 2026-05-20 and covers roughly half of paid hours. Every throughput figure is a pooled tier average, which is the right way to use noisy logs — but it means no single order can be costed reliably from this data.
  • Order-level costing was attempted and rejected. About 3% of orders imply impossible rates (0.2 to 283 pcs/hr) purely from logging noise. Pooling averages that out; per-order figures inherit it.
  • No period-correct historical cost exists. There is no 2016 general ledger or TimeClick data, so the ten-year section applies today's prices and costs to ten years of real order shapes. It answers “how would today's pricing have fared against our actual history” — not “what did we earn in 2016”.
  • Per-unit revenue in mixed cap/garment orders is split proportionally by unit count, which flatters caps and understates garments. Treat those $/unit columns as indicative, not line-accurate.
  • Purchase-order coverage varies by year, so blank-price bands are less reliable in the earliest years than the most recent ones.
  • Two earlier spreadsheet recommendations were price cuts of 44–68% on our best work ($6.75 a logo where the engine charges $12–18 and we realize $28.58; $3.25 a patch where we charge $10). They should not be revived — measured throughput contradicts both.
